The Effects of Algorithmic Cues on Judgements of Learning

Lucas R. Betts*, Skylar J. Laursen, Trent N. Cash, and Evan F. Risko
UNIVERSITY OF WATERLOO
*Contact: lrbetts@uwaterloo.ca

IntroductionExperiment 1Experiment 2ConclusionsOriginal poster

Introduction

Theoretical Framework:

According to Koriat’s (1997) Cue-Utilization Theory, Judgments of Learning (JOLs) are inferred from a variety of cues: Intrinsic (e.g., Properties of the material); Extrinsic (e.g., Learning conditions); and Mnemonic Cues (e.g., Subjective experiences).

Current Study:

Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces a novel type of cue. Specifically, AI can provide a JOL for an individual – a kind of external algorithmic cue. Here, we examine how individuals use such a cue by including AI predictions in a standard JOL task. In addition, to examine how the AI JOL impacts the use of other metamemory cues, we included a font size manipulation (Rhodes & Castel, 2008). Crucially, AI predictions showed no font-size effect, providing a competing cue and a means of detecting the integration of the AI cue.

Research Question / Hypotheses:

To what extent do learners use information provided by an AI system (AI-JOL) when making metamemory judgments?

H1: If learners ignore the AI, then the magnitude of the font-size effect should be unaffected by the provision of the AI prediction. This might indicate that individuals do not believe the AI can provide useful information about their learning.

H2: If learners use the AI in place of generating their own judgement, then the font-size effect should be eliminated. This offloading of the metamemory judgement would be consistent with individuals minimizing cognitive effort.

H3: If learners integrate both cues, then font size will still influence JOLs, but the effect may be attenuated when the AI prediction is provided. This would be consistent with work demonstrating that individuals will integrate multiple cues (Undorf et al., 2018).

Experiment 1

Methods:

Within-Subjects Design (N = 86, Mage = 18.9 (range 17-22) , 66 Females: 20 Males)

Stimuli:

Source of AI: Derived from weighted aggregated JOL data from previous experiments (M = 56.98, SD = 11.70).

Font Size: The provided AI predictions were constant across font sizes.

Procedure:

48 words. AI-JOLs appeared with the JOL prompt after each word disappeared. Participants made JOLs, completed a 5-min math distractor, then a 4-min free recall test.

Results:

JOLs (Figure 1)

A significant main effect of font size: participants reported higher JOLs for larger words, F(1,83) = 28.70, p < .001, ηP2 = .019.

The presence of the AI did not shift participants’ JOLs, F(1,83) = 1.15, p = .27, ηP2 < .001, nor did it attenuate the font size effect, F(1,83) = 0.06, p = .80, ηP2 < .001.

AI Alignment (Figure 2)

AI Alignment was calculated as a Pearson correlation for each participant between their JOLs and the AI-JOLs across trials.

If participants were completely ignoring the AI, then their AI alignment should remain unaffected by the AI-JOLs' presence.

AI alignment significantly increased when the AI was present compared to when it was absent, t(83) = 2.24, p = .027, 95% CI [.007, .12], d = .25.

Features of Experiment 1 (Rationale for Experiment 2)

Participants largely ignored the AI (E1), possibly due to features of the experimental context. Experiment 2 introduced three key changes to test if learners integrate AI under different conditions:

Timing: Shifted AI presentation to occur with the target word.

Consistency: Provided the AI cue consistently on every trial.

Source: Utilized recall-derived estimates to introduce a larger discrepancy that systematically fell below learners’ initial guesses.

Experiment 2

Methods:

Mixed Design (N = 228, Mage = 37.8 (range 18-75) , 82 Females: 118 Males : 12 Not Listed).

AI condition manipulated between-subjects (nAI With = 110, nAI None = 102).

Stimuli:

Source of AI: Derived from recall performance data from Experiment 1 (M = 26.88, SD = 14.27).

Procedure:

48 words. AI-JOLs appeared with the target word or not at all. Participants made JOLs, completed a 5-min math distractor, then a 4-min free recall test.

Results:

JOLs (Figure 3)

Font size had a significant main effect: participants reported higher JOLs for larger words, F(1,210) = 39.39, p < .001, ηP2 = .006.

AI condition had a significant main effect: participants reported lower JOLs when the AI-JOL was given, F(1,210) = 23.28, p < .001, ηP2 = .010.

The interaction between font size and AI condition was significant, F(1,210) = 6.65, p = .011, ηP2 = .001.

Discussion / Conclusions

Experiment 1 (AI Ignored): AI presence did not attenuate the font-size effect; thus, learners largely ignored the AI.

Experiment 2 (AI Integrated): Learners integrated the AI predictions, which significantly attenuated the font-size effect.

What Makes AI Predictions Influential?

The integration of AI-JOLs is likely driven by three key factors:

Timing: Advice may be more impactful when presented concurrently during initial encoding, potentially allowing learners to evaluate the item and the advice together before forming an independent estimate.

Consistency: Consistent availability of the AI cue may help learners develop a reliable strategy for incorporating it.

Discrepancy: A larger discrepancy that challenges, rather than exceeds, a learner’s initial guess may prompt greater consideration and re-evaluation by the learner.
